overview: Nekoware v1's Speed is a two-mode movement pinner. Vanilla mode writes the Speed setting (default 1, range 0-5) into the motion every tick and, whenever the player is moving on ground, multiplies it by 1.25 and stamps motionY to 0.42 for a jump. Verus mode pins 0.42 on ground with the same 0.42 jump and 0.36 in air, fixed constants that ignore the Speed setting entirely. A Flag Check toggle watches for S08PacketPlayerPosLook and, when the server teleports the player, prints a chat message and toggles the module off, a self-disable on setback rather than a bypass. The module also instantiates a DynamicFriction field it never uses and registers an empty UpdateEvent handler, both dead code.

sections.p: The MovementEvent handler for Vanilla mode calls MovementUtils.setMoveSpeed with the Speed setting on every event, pinning the horizontal magnitude unconditionally, and then checks isMovingOnGround: while the player is moving and grounded it re-pins at 1.25 times the setting and writes motionY 0.42 through both event.setY and the motion field. The effect is a ground tick that jumps every tick, exactly the bunny-hop cadence, with the horizontal magnitude held at 1.25 blocks per tick at the default setting. The write-through goes to the motion fields that the movement event then carries into the C03 stream.

Verus mode ignores the Speed setting and uses two fixed constants: 0.42 while moving on ground with the same 0.42 jump stamp, and 0.36 while airborne. The mode name advertises the target anticheat, and the constants are tuned to the Verus-era expectation of a 0.42 hop with a 0.36 air pin, which is below the 0.42 jump but still well above vanilla sprint speed. Unlike the Vanilla mode there is no multiplier branch, so the entire mode is two setMoveSpeed calls and one jump stamp, the simplest possible bhop pin.

The PacketInEvent handler watches S08PacketPlayerPosLook whenever the Flag Check boolean is on, prints "Speed disabled because you flagged!" through ChatUtil and calls toggle() to switch the module off. That is a retreat-on-setback design: the first server teleport kills the module instead of fighting the correction, which is why the module never enters a teleport fight with the anticheat. Two dead-code findings complete the picture: the DynamicFriction field dynamicNCPFriction is constructed but never referenced, and the UpdateEvent handler is registered with an empty body, so the only live logic is the movement handler and the S08 watcher.

files.label: Speed.java (module)
files.explanation: The module file is the complete behavior. The MovementEvent handler implements both modes with the setMoveSpeed calls and the 0.42 jump stamp, the PacketInEvent handler implements the S08 Flag Check self-disable, and the constructor registers the modes and settings. The dead DynamicFriction field and the empty UpdateEvent handler are documented in the sections. The file also shows the exact pin values, 1.25 times the Speed setting on ground in Vanilla mode and the fixed 0.42 and 0.36 in Verus mode, which are the numbers every countering check measures against.

files.label: MovementUtils.java (motion pinning)
files.explanation: setMoveSpeed is the mechanism the module lives on: it reads the movement input, normalizes forward and strafe, blends diagonals with the fixed 0.6398355709958845 sine factor, and writes motionX and motionZ directly from the yaw. The module calls the single-argument overload, which targets the motion fields, not the event, so the pin survives into whatever packet the movement system emits. The utility also carries the TargetStrafe coupling, reading Aura.currentEntity and TargetStrafe.dir when target strafing is active, which means the pin direction can be hijacked by the killaura module's current target during combat.

countering.label: SurvivalFly (horizontal speed envelope)
countering.explanation:
NCP's SurvivalFly is the horizontal speed check in this tree; there is no dedicated moving Speed class. check() derives the allowance from prepareSpeedEstimation, which predicts the per-tick distance from walk speed, friction and the sprint 30 percent adder, and handlePredictableMove compares the actual horizontal distance against the allowed one, with the violation computed as the sum of horizontal and vertical overage times 100 and a set-back on failure. The Vanilla mode at the default setting pins 1.25 blocks per tick against a predicted sprint of roughly 0.28 to 0.31, so the first grounded move after the pin produces an offset near 0.95 and a violation in the nineties, an immediate set-back.

The vertical side does not rescue it: the 0.42 jump is exactly vanilla and is accepted through the jump envelope, which arms data.jumpDelay, but the horizontal pin is the whole problem. Verus mode's 0.42 ground pin and 0.36 air pin are lower, yet still above the predicted sprint allowance, so both modes violate on the first move and the Flag Check self-disable is the only mitigation the module offers, turning the module off after the first setback instead of surviving it.

countering.label: Speed (BunnyHop and onGround expected)
countering.explanation:
Arc v2's moving Speed check models the bunny-hop envelope from config defaults of block 0.6699 and a base move speed of 0.2873. On the ground branch, expected is thisMove divided by groundTime plus the base, with groundTime capped at 8, and sustained movement above that flags under the onground_expected name once groundTicks reach 5. The Vanilla mode's 1.25 blocks per tick versus 1.25 over 8 plus 0.2873 equals roughly 0.44 is a flag on the first grounded window, and the constant re-jump keeps the ground branch from ever clearing.

Verus mode is the tuned case and the honest boundary: the 0.36 air pin sits below the off-ground descending expectation of 0.2873 plus 0.08, so it passes the descending ticks, while the 0.42 ground pin exceeds the expected ground value and accumulates through the groundTicks counter. The mode buys a few ticks of air grace before the descending stage catches the 0.42 hop's horizontal carry, which is the narrow pass surface the Verus constants were chosen to exploit.

countering.label: Speed (momentum conservation)
countering.explanation:
Hawk's movement Speed check conserves momentum: expected is friction times the previous speed plus the maximum force and the small adders, where friction is the block slipperiness on ground and 0.91 in air, and the sprint-jump adder contributes the vanilla 0.2. Discrepancy accumulates per player across moves and flags when the total exceeds 0.1, with the violation scaled by ten. The Vanilla mode's 1.25 pin against a ground expectation near 0.33 leaves a discrepancy around 0.9 on the first grounded move, so the very first updatePos after the pin flags and rubberbands.

The STRAFE-style ratchet is absent here but irrelevant: even the Verus mode's 0.42 ground pin leaves a discrepancy above the threshold once the 0.2 sprint-jump adder is consumed, and the 0.36 air pin stays above the friction-decayed expectation during the fall. The jump and step exemptions only forgive the vanilla 0.2 adder, never a magnitude pinned above it, so neither mode configures out of the accumulator.

countering.label: SurvivalFly (S08 flag-check interaction)
countering.explanation:
This entry documents the module's Flag Check against the same NCP file that issues the setbacks. SurvivalFly's handleViolation returns the player to a stored set-back location through an S08 teleport, and the module's PacketInEvent handler watches for exactly that packet, prints the flag message and toggles itself off. The interaction is a race: NCP fires the S08 within the same tick the violation accumulates, and the module's retreat only guarantees it will not keep re-pinning afterward, it does nothing about the violation already scored or the set-back already applied.

The honest summary is that Flag Check converts a sustained violation stream into a single violation plus a self-disable, which is why a Nekoware user sees one teleport and then no more flags rather than a chain. The check itself is unaffected, which is the point of the entry: the countering pressure works exactly as designed, and the module's only defense is to stop cheating after the first detection.
